aji-keshi.title: aji-keshi
aji-keshi.definition: Aji-keshi ("erasing the aji") in weiqi is playing a move that forces the opponent to answer in a way that removes the player's own latent options — the residual aji a position was carrying. It is one of the most characteristic strong-player errors: the move usually gains something locally, but it spends a possibility that was worth more unspent.
aji-keshi.elaboration: As a proposal in the section's own Weiqi Strategic Theory (§4), aji-keshi is a premature settlement: a move that drives a cell held at an unwitnessed value (⊥) to true or false and thereby destroys the option that cell was carrying, so it is not a bad move because it loses points locally — it usually gains points locally — but because it collapses a ⊥ that was worth more open than closed. Status: proposal.

related.title: aji
related.note: Aji-keshi is the specific error of destroying aji rather than merely leaving it unused.

related.title: gote
related.note: Aji-keshi sequences are frequently gote: the local gain does not carry the initiative forward.

related.title: honte
related.note: Honte deliberately spends tempo instead of aji; aji-keshi spends aji instead of tempo.

aji.title: aji
aji.definition: Aji — literally "taste" — in weiqi is latent potential: the residual possibilities in dead or weak stones, or in a defect in the opponent's shape, that are not currently playable but that constrain what both sides can do. The standard maxim is that aji is used by not using it — a threat that has already been played is no longer a threat.
aji.elaboration: The section's Weiqi Strategic Theory note (§4) proposes the Obsmetrologia inconsistency sheaf as aji's formal home: aji as a cell held at an unwitnessed value (⊥) whose option value is a function of remaining unwitnessed, so that aji-keshi is the move that prematurely settles that cell and spends the option — status: proposal, that note's own.

related.title: aji-keshi
related.note: Aji-keshi is the error of spending aji's option value for a small, immediate, and usually forced gain.

related.title: sente
related.note: Unlike sente, whose value is spent the instant it is played, aji's value depends on staying unplayed.

related.title: honte
related.note: Honte is the move that trades away the aji a lighter move would have left behind.

area-scoring.title: area-scoring
area-scoring.definition: Area scoring in weiqi computes each player's final score as the number of that player's own live stones remaining on the board plus the vacant points that count as that player's territory; captures made during play matter only insofar as they change which stones are on the board at the end, not as separately counted prisoner points. Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules all use area scoring. Because a stone on the board and an enclosed empty point are worth the same one point each, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs nothing under area scoring: it simply converts a territory point into a stone point.
area-scoring.elaboration: That single property is the main practical difference from territory-scoring, and it is why area-scoring rulesets can set standard komi a half-point to a full point higher than territory-scoring rulesets covering the same game: Black, moving first, typically ends a game with one more stone on the board than White, and area scoring counts that stone directly where territory scoring would not. The exact standard komi for each ruleset is recorded in the rulesets comparison.

related.title: territory
related.note: Area scoring counts a player's territory as part of the total, alongside that player's own stones.

related.title: territory-scoring
related.note: Area scoring and territory scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.

related.title: komi
related.note: Standard komi values differ between area-scoring and territory-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.

related.title: dead-stones
related.note: Area-scoring rulesets typically resolve disputed dead stones by resuming play to an actual capture.

related.title: pass
related.note: Some area-scoring implementations reconcile counts with territory scoring using a pass stone.

atari.title: atari
atari.definition: Atari in weiqi is the state in which a stone or connected group has only one liberty remaining and is therefore under immediate threat of capture.
atari.elaboration: Atari matters because it turns a broad positional game into a forced tactical problem. When a group falls to one liberty, the next move often becomes urgent for both players: one side tries to capture, while the other tries to extend, connect, or create shape.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Atari is defined by the reduction to a single remaining liberty.

related.title: capture
related.note: A capture follows if the threatened group cannot answer the atari.

related.title: connection
related.note: Connecting to another group is one common way to escape atari.

capture.title: capture
capture.definition: A capture in weiqi occurs when a move removes the last liberty from an opposing stone or connected group, after which those stones are removed from the board.
capture.elaboration: Capture is the game's basic tactical enforcement rule. Without it, enclosure would carry no force. But weiqi is not a pure capture race, because players usually capture in order to secure shape, reduce influence, or stabilize territory, not only to remove material.

related.title: atari
related.note: Atari is the immediate threat state that often precedes capture.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Capture is defined by the removal of the last liberty.

related.title: life and death
related.note: Many life-and-death problems end by proving whether capture can be forced.

related.title: territory
related.note: Captures often matter because they change which empty points can become territory.

related.title: ko
related.note: Some captures trigger ko and cannot be answered by immediate recapture.

connection.title: connection
connection.definition: A connection in weiqi is a relation between stones that makes them function as one group, sharing liberties and supporting each other's defense.
connection.elaboration: Connection is structurally important because isolated stones are weak. A move that does not gain immediate territory may still be strong if it joins two unsettled groups, prevents a cutting attack, or turns a fragile shape into one that can live.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Connected stones share liberties, which is why connection increases strength.

related.title: eye
related.note: A connected group often tries to make eyes as one unit rather than as isolated stones.

related.title: life and death
related.note: Many life-and-death problems turn on whether stones can stay connected.

dame.title: dame
dame.definition: Dame in weiqi are the neutral, empty points left on the board that border stones of both colors and belong to neither player's territory.
dame.elaboration: Whether it is worth spending a move to fill a dame depends entirely on which scoring system is being used, which is why the term matters more than its small size suggests. Under **area scoring** (the family that includes Chinese rules), the final count adds up living stones on the board plus surrounded territory. A stone played on a dame is a stone on the board, so it is worth exactly one point, the same as a stone played anywhere else legal. Leaving dame unfilled when the opponent can still fill them is therefore a real, countable loss.

related.title: pass
related.note: Passing before all dame are filled can cost a point under area scoring, one reason passing is timed carefully.

related.title: territory
related.note: Dame are defined by what they are not: nobody's secured territory.

related.title: komi
related.note: Because komi is a fixed score adjustment, it does not change how dame are counted, only what the resulting total is compared against.

related.title: capture
related.note: A dame can turn into a live point for one side if a nearby capture changes which stones actually stand.

dango.title: dango
dango.definition: Dango ("dumpling") in weiqi is a clump of stones bunched together with few liberties relative to their number, an overconcentrated shape that gains little board coverage for the stones spent on it. A dumpling shape is inefficient specifically because it duplicates work: several stones end up defending the same small set of liberties that fewer, better-placed stones would have secured.
dango.elaboration: Dango is not the same failure as being merely heavy. Thickness is also a concentration of stones, but a thick wall faces outward and does useful work on the position around it; a dumpling shape faces nowhere in particular and is judged a mistake independent of context. Avoiding dango is one of the standard reasons to prefer tobi or keima over a solid connection when either would hold the position.

related.title: thickness
related.note: Thickness is a concentration of stones that still does useful outward-facing work; dango is the same concentration without it.

related.title: tobi
related.note: Playing tobi instead of a solid connection is a standard way to avoid building dango.

related.title: keima
related.note: Keima, like tobi, covers ground a solid connection would spend into dango.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Sabaki explicitly favors light shape over the heavy, clumped shape dango names.

dead-stones.title: dead-stones
dead-stones.definition: Dead stones in weiqi are stones left on the board after both players pass that cannot avoid eventual capture under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test life-and-death reading always applies: it cannot make two secure eyes and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in seki and is never marked dead.
dead-stones.elaboration: How dead stones are settled is one of the sharpest procedural differences between rulesets, and one the rulesets comparison records explicitly. Japanese-style rules settle status by mutual agreement after the two passes, which is fast but is the classic source of scoring disputes when players disagree about a group's fate. Chinese-style area-scoring play resolves genuine disagreements by resuming alternating play until the disputed group is actually captured or clearly alive, which is slower but leaves no room for disagreement about the result.

related.title: life-and-death
related.note: A stone is dead exactly when life-and-death reading shows it cannot live.

related.title: pass
related.note: Dead-stone settlement begins only after both players have passed in succession.

related.title: seki
related.note: Stones in seki are explicitly not dead; they survive by sharing unfillable liberties.

related.title: area-scoring
related.note: Area-scoring rulesets typically settle disputed dead stones by resuming capture, not by agreement.

related.title: territory-scoring
related.note: Territory-scoring rulesets typically settle dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.

eye.title: eye
eye.definition: An eye in weiqi is an empty point or enclosed space inside a group's shape that functions as an internal liberty and helps determine whether the group can live.
eye.elaboration: Eyes matter because they change the status of a group. A surrounded group with no secure eye shape may still be dead, while a well-connected group with two separate eyes is usually safe. This is why players often defend shape even when no immediate capture is on the board.

related.title: liberty
related.note: An eye is a protected internal liberty.

related.title: connection
related.note: Strong connection makes it easier for a group to form stable eyes.

related.title: life and death
related.note: Life-and-death reading asks whether a group can make enough eyes to survive.

false-eye.title: false-eye
false-eye.definition: A false eye in weiqi is an eye-shaped empty point that looks like a protected internal liberty but does not meet the diagonal-control and connection requirements of a real eye, so the opponent can eventually force the surrounding group to fill it.
false-eye.elaboration: An eye stays real only if the stones around it are firmly connected and enough of the diagonal points next to it are also controlled by the same color: one diagonal for an eye in the corner, two on the edge, and three in the center of the board. A false eye fails one of these conditions. Often the surrounding stones can be cut apart, or too many of the diagonal points belong to the opponent. Once the opponent captures a cutting stone or occupies enough diagonals, the eye point stops being a safe internal liberty and becomes an ordinary point that the surrounding group may eventually have to fill itself, or that the opponent can play into without dying.

related.title: eye
related.note: A false eye is an eye-shaped point that fails the diagonal-control and connection tests that make a real eye secure.

related.title: life and death
related.note: Distinguishing true eyes from false eyes is a routine step in life-and-death reading.

related.title: connection
related.note: A false eye often results from a weak connection among the stones that surround it.

related.title: liberty
related.note: A false eye is not a reliably protected liberty, unlike a true eye.

fuseki.title: fuseki
fuseki.definition: Fuseki in weiqi is the opening considered as a whole board, as distinct from joseki, the memorized locally-balanced corner sequences a fuseki is built from. Where a joseki is judged by whether it is locally balanced, a fuseki is judged by whether the whole-board framework it builds serves the position — a joseki that is correct in isolation can still be the wrong choice for the fuseki around it.
fuseki.elaboration: Fuseki theory carries the same historical dispute as influence: territorial orthodoxy took the corners first, then the sides, then the centre; the New Fuseki (*Shinfuseki*) movement of Go Seigen and Kitani Minoru, 1933, argued for centre-facing, influence-first opening play instead, and permanently changed what counted as a reasonable opening even though parts of it were later shown to be wrong. Choosing between these is the "direction of play" judgment the section's Weiqi Strategic Theory note names as the concept most resistant to local analysis and the one professionals most consistently identify as the amateur's real weakness.

related.title: joseki
related.note: A fuseki is built from joseki chosen to fit the whole board, not merely to be locally correct.

related.title: influence
related.note: The New Fuseki movement is the historical dispute over how much influence a fuseki should stake on, versus territory taken directly.

related.title: thickness
related.note: A fuseki that builds thickness is choosing influence-first play over immediate territory.

geta.title: geta
geta.definition: Geta ("net") in weiqi is a technique for capturing a stone or small group by surrounding it loosely, from a distance, with a small number of stones placed so that any attempt to extend toward a liberty runs into a stone already in place. The captured stones are never chased liberty by liberty; the net is set once, and the group inside it cannot escape by any single move.
geta.elaboration: A net differs from a direct chase in exactly this way: it needs no follow-up reading once it is set correctly, whereas a ladder-style pursuit must be read all the way to its end to confirm it works. A poorly placed net leaves a gap the enclosed stones can escape through, so confirming a geta still requires reading the specific shape — it is a shape recognized and verified, not merely assumed from the general pattern.

related.title: capture
related.note: A net is one specific technique for forcing a capture without a direct chase.

related.title: atari
related.note: The enclosed stones need never be placed in atari for a net to work; the net closes off their escape before that stage.

related.title: liberty
related.note: A net is set by occupying the liberties an escaping stone would otherwise extend toward.

gote.title: gote
gote.definition: Gote in weiqi is a move that ends the mover's turn because the opponent need not answer it. It is the complement of sente: where a sente sequence lets its player keep the initiative and play elsewhere next, a gote sequence hands the initiative to the opponent.
gote.elaboration: Gote is not simply a worse outcome than sente; it is a distinct position in Berlekamp and Wolfe's combinatorial-game-theory treatment of the endgame, where a position decomposes into a disjunctive sum of independent local games, each with a temperature, and the sente/gote distinction falls directly out of that temperature structure rather than being judged move by move. A large gote play can still be worth more than a small sente play; the two are compared by their values, not by category alone.

related.title: sente
related.note: Gote is the complementary state to sente: a move that ends the initiative rather than keeping it.

related.title: miai
related.note: Miai converts a point that would otherwise force a sente/gote choice into one that can be ignored by both sides.

related.title: aji-keshi
related.note: A gote move that spends latent potential for a small local gain is the classic aji-keshi error.

handicap.title: handicap
handicap.definition: A handicap in weiqi is a rule adjustment, usually extra Black stones placed before play begins, that lets players of unequal strength compete in a meaningful game.
handicap.elaboration: Handicap is one reason weiqi supports play across large skill differences without becoming a different game. The stronger player does not receive more pieces or special powers during play. Instead, the weaker player begins from a materially stronger board position.

related.title: komi
related.note: Komi balances even games, while handicap balances unequal players.

related.title: territory
related.note: Handicap stones reshape the territorial balance from the first move.

related.title: connection
related.note: Handicap stones are useful only if the weaker player can connect them into efficient whole-board structure.

honte.title: honte
honte.definition: Honte in weiqi is the solid, "proper" move — the one that leaves no aji behind, at the cost of a little tempo. Kageyama's *Lessons in the Fundamentals of Go* is the standard source on honte, alongside shape and direction of play, and the concept exists specifically to name the trade a greedier, more aji-leaving move refuses to make.
honte.elaboration: Honte is a judgment call rather than a rule: playing honte everywhere would waste tempo on threats the opponent could never have exploited, while never playing honte leaves aji that eventually costs more than the tempo it would have taken to remove.

related.title: aji
related.note: Honte is the move that spends tempo specifically to avoid leaving aji.

related.title: aji-keshi
related.note: Honte trades tempo for safety; aji-keshi trades aji for a smaller local gain, and is the error honte is meant to avoid on the other side.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Honte and sabaki are opposite responses to local pressure: solidity everywhere versus expendable lightness.

hoshi.title: hoshi
hoshi.definition: Hoshi in weiqi are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen.
hoshi.elaboration: Hoshi matter for two distinct reasons. First, they are the standard locations for handicap stones: the fixed Japanese placement pattern seats every handicap stone, from two up to nine, on one of these nine points, and the tengen point is the fifth and seventh stone added as handicaps increase (see Handicap Placement and Komi Values for the full placement order). Second, even outside handicap games, the corner hoshi mark a natural opening frame: a stone on the 4-4 point does not by itself secure the corner the way a 3-3 point does, trading that immediate territory for speed and center-facing influence, which is why it is one of the most common corner openings for beginners to learn even though the 3-4 point (komoku) is usually described as the more evenly balanced choice between territory and influence.

related.title: handicap
related.note: Hoshi are the fixed points on which handicap stones are placed.

related.title: komi
related.note: Komi is the scoring counterpart to handicap placement on the hoshi.

related.title: territory
related.note: A hoshi stone's opening value comes from how evenly it can grow into territory.

influence.title: influence
influence.definition: Influence (*seiryoku*) in weiqi is the effect a stone or group exerts on the space around it without enclosing it. It is not territory-in-waiting, and treating it as such is the classical beginner error: influence's value is that it constrains the opponent's options, making invasions in its neighbourhood expensive or unlivable, so the opponent must play elsewhere while the influence-holder collects the difference.
influence.elaboration: Influence has carried a genuine, unresolved theory dispute since the game's earliest written strategy. Territorial orthodoxy through the early twentieth century took the corners first, then the sides, then the centre, valuing the corner highest because the board edges do the enclosing work for free. The New Fuseki (*Shinfuseki*) movement of 1933 argued the opposite: centre-facing, influence-first opening play. The AI era beginning in 2016 rebalanced both camps' settled judgments without producing a single human-legible theory of why — professional play had undervalued influence in some positions and overvalued it in others, with no simple direction. A lesson that teaches only the pre-2016 evaluations as settled fact teaches several things now known to be wrong.

related.title: thickness
related.note: Thickness is influence's settled, wall-shaped special case.

related.title: territory
related.note: Influence is not territory-in-waiting; the two are frequently confused and are strategically distinct.

related.title: fuseki
related.note: The New Fuseki movement is the historical dispute over how much influence a whole-board opening should stake on.

related.title: joseki
related.note: Several long-canonical joseki were revalued in the AI era precisely on influence/territory balance.

joseki.title: joseki
joseki.definition: Joseki in weiqi are the memorized, locally-balanced corner sequences catalogued across the standard literature, most exhaustively by Ishida's three-volume *Dictionary of Basic Joseki*. Each joseki is a locally complete exchange in which neither side gains a clear local advantage; the players agree, in effect, to a fair local trade and both move on.
joseki.elaboration: The essential caveat belongs with the definition: joseki are locally balanced and therefore whole-board-neutral by construction. That is why "knowing joseki" is famously worth little on its own — the sequence that is correct in one whole-board context can be the wrong one to play in another, and choosing which corner sequence fits the position in front of a player is a direction-of-play judgment the dictionary itself cannot make. The AI era additionally showed several long-canonical joseki to be slightly worse for one side than professional play had assumed for decades.

related.title: fuseki
related.note: Fuseki is the whole-board opening a joseki must be chosen to fit; a joseki correct in isolation can still be the wrong choice for the fuseki around it.

related.title: influence
related.note: AI-era analysis revalued several joseki specifically on the influence/territory balance they leave.

related.title: miai
related.note: Many joseki sequences end by leaving the two players a miai choice between equivalent local continuations.

keima.title: keima
keima.definition: Keima ("knight's move") in weiqi is playing a stone one point away from an existing stone in one direction and two points away in the perpendicular direction, the same offset a knight moves on a chessboard. Like tobi, it is not a physical connection; it covers ground faster than a solid connection at the cost of a gap the opponent can, in principle, exploit.
keima.elaboration: The "knight's move cut," playing directly into the gap keima leaves, is the standard test of the shape: whether it actually works depends on the surrounding position, since the cutting stone itself often lands in trouble the keima's owner can exploit in turn. A keima that cannot be cut without loss is, for practical purposes, as solid as a direct connection while covering more board.

related.title: tobi
related.note: Tobi is the other standard light-extension shape, covering a straight-line offset rather than keima's diagonal one.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Keima's speed over solid connection makes it a characteristic move of sabaki play.

kikashi.title: kikashi
kikashi.definition: Kikashi in weiqi is a forcing move played for the value of the response it compels rather than for the stone's own local worth, kept as a quick exchange rather than developed further. The player spends one move, the opponent must answer it in a fixed way, and the player keeps sente to play elsewhere — the exchange is judged complete the moment it is made.
kikashi.elaboration: Kikashi is the opposite outcome from aji-keshi: both are forcing moves, but a kikashi is worth more played than left unplayed, while an aji-keshi is worth less played than left unplayed. Distinguishing the two requires reading whether the forced response removes an option the player would rather have kept open; a move that looks like kikashi in one position is aji-keshi in another, depending on what the position still needs from the point being forced.

related.title: sente
related.note: Kikashi is specifically a forcing move whose value is realized entirely through keeping sente, not through the stone's local presence.

related.title: aji-keshi
related.note: Aji-keshi is the failure mode kikashi is judged against: the same forcing shape, spent when it should have stayed unplayed.

related.title: sute-ishi
related.note: A kikashi stone is frequently also a sacrifice stone, left to be captured once its forcing work is done.

ko.title: ko
ko.definition: Ko in weiqi is a repetition constraint that forbids a player from making the immediate recapture that would recreate the previous board position.
ko.elaboration: Ko matters because it prevents endless local loops while preserving the tactical possibility of capture. Once a ko appears, the fight usually stops being purely local: the blocked player must move elsewhere first, which can turn the rest of the board into leverage for the eventual return to the ko point.

related.title: superko
related.note: Superko generalizes this simple ko rule to forbid recreating any earlier board position, not only the position from one move ago.

related.title: capture
related.note: Ko arises from a specific kind of capture and attempted recapture.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Ko positions usually appear when liberties are reduced to a narrow exchange.

related.title: atari
related.note: Many ko fights begin from repeated atari and recapture threats.

related.title: territory
related.note: Ko fights often matter because the threatened capture would change important territory.

komi.title: komi
komi.definition: Komi in weiqi is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage.
komi.elaboration: Komi matters because weiqi is asymmetrical at the start: Black moves first. Without compensation, that initiative would distort results across many even games. Komi is therefore a scoring adjustment, not a tactical rule inside local fights.

related.title: territory
related.note: Komi is added during final scoring after territory and other points are counted.

related.title: capture
related.note: Captures may affect the final score that komi then adjusts.

related.title: handicap
related.note: Handicap changes the starting position, while komi adjusts the score.

liberty.title: liberty
liberty.definition: A liberty in weiqi is an empty intersection directly adjacent to a stone or connected group of stones. Liberties determine whether a group remains on the board. When the last liberty is removed, the group is subject to capture.
liberty.elaboration: Liberties matter because they convert board geometry into tactical pressure. A move may look quiet in territorial terms while still being urgent if it reduces a group from two liberties to one. This is why local fights in weiqi often turn on counting available adjacent points rather than on the nominal size of a group.

related.title: atari
related.note: Atari is the urgent state in which only one liberty remains.

related.title: capture
related.note: Capture happens when a stone or group loses its final liberty.

related.title: connection
related.note: Connections matter because they let stones share liberties.

related.title: territory
related.note: Securing territory often depends on keeping enough liberties to prevent invasion and capture.

related.title: ko
related.note: Ko can arise when a single-stone capture would otherwise repeat because liberties are exchanged back and forth.

life-and-death.title: life-and-death
life-and-death.definition: Life and death in weiqi is the analysis of whether a group can secure enough stable shape, usually through eyes, to avoid capture, or whether the opponent can force it off the board.
life-and-death.elaboration: Life-and-death reading is one of the game's central skills because local shape decides global outcomes. A large territorial framework can collapse if one key group dies. A small group can become strategically decisive if it lives inside the opponent's area.

related.title: eye
related.note: Eyes are the main structural feature used to determine whether a group lives.

related.title: connection
related.note: Connected stones defend and build eye shape more effectively than scattered stones.

related.title: atari
related.note: Atari is the immediate tactical pressure that often precedes life-and-death resolution.

miai.title: miai
miai.definition: Miai in weiqi are two points of equal value such that, if the opponent takes one, the player takes the other. Miai converts a contested point into a settled one: once two points are miai, a player can safely ignore both, playing elsewhere, and answer only after the opponent commits to one.
miai.elaboration: Miai is the most directly formalizable concept of the section's classical strategy vocabulary, and the section's own Weiqi Strategic Theory note explicitly declines to reach for a house formalism for it: a prior corpus note already rejected a sheaf-gluing reading of miai, so the entry defines it plainly rather than adding machinery.

related.title: sente
related.note: A miai point never needs to be taken in sente, since either side taking it settles the exchange.

related.title: gote
related.note: Miai removes the sente/gote choice a contested point would otherwise force.

related.title: joseki
related.note: Many joseki sequences end by leaving the two players a miai choice between locally equivalent continuations.

moyo.title: moyo
moyo.definition: Moyo in weiqi is a large-scale framework of potential territory, outlined by stones' influence rather than enclosed by them. A moyo is influence organized at whole-board scale and aimed at a specific outcome — growing into secured space — where bare influence only constrains the opponent's options without claiming any of them.
moyo.elaboration: A moyo is not territory. It remains open to invasion or reduction until the framework is actually closed, and a large moyo that cannot be defended once entered is the classical trap of the style: the framework looked large on the board but could not survive contact. Whether a given moyo is worth more than the territory an opponent secures while invading it is a genuine, position-dependent judgment, not a rule of thumb.

related.title: influence
related.note: Moyo is influence organized into one large, whole-board framework rather than a local effect.

related.title: territory
related.note: Moyo is territory-in-potential; it is not secured until the framework survives invasion.

related.title: thickness
related.note: A moyo often grows outward from a thick wall, though the wall's value and the framework's value are judged separately.

pass.title: pass
pass.definition: A pass in weiqi is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by ko, suicide, or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open dead-stones settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture.
pass.elaboration: Passing is where the two major scoring conventions attach a small but real procedural difference. Under strict territory scoring, a pass costs nothing. Under some area-scoring implementations, and under the AGA's hybrid counting method specifically, each pass hands the opponent a stone (a "pass stone") to be placed in the passer's own territory before counting, which is precisely the device that keeps area-scoring and territory-scoring results aligned.

related.title: dead-stones
related.note: The pair of passes that ends play is what starts dead-stone settlement.

related.title: area-scoring
related.note: Some area-scoring implementations use a pass stone to keep area and territory counts consistent.

related.title: territory-scoring
related.note: Territory scoring is the convention the pass stone device was designed to stay consistent with.

related.title: seki
related.note: A seki is left unresolved through passing; neither side plays its shared liberties before the game ends.

sabaki.title: sabaki
sabaki.definition: Sabaki in weiqi is making a light, flexible, quickly-settled shape inside the opponent's sphere of influence, playing so that any individual stone is expendable. It contrasts with heavy (*omoi*) shape, which must be saved at all costs and therefore becomes a target the opponent can attack repeatedly for profit.
sabaki.elaboration: Sabaki is a posture more than a single move: a group played for sabaki accepts that some of its stones may be sacrificed, and treats that as acceptable so long as the group as a whole settles with enough shape to survive or to have profited elsewhere while the opponent was attacking it. It is a compressed way of getting an approximate answer to a local fight without doing the full life-and-death calculation a heavier group would demand.

related.title: thickness
related.note: Sabaki is the light-shape alternative to confronting an opponent's thickness directly.

related.title: influence
related.note: Sabaki is specifically the posture for operating inside the opponent's influence rather than outside it.

related.title: honte
related.note: Honte and sabaki are opposite responses to the same pressure: honte spends a move to remove all weakness, sabaki accepts weakness as expendable.

seki.title: seki
seki.definition: Seki in weiqi is a standoff in which two or more groups of opposite color share their remaining liberties, and neither side can play into the shared liberties without reducing its own group to a liberty count the opponent can then capture on the next move. Neither group has two eyes, yet neither can be captured either, so both remain on the board unresolved for the rest of the game. Seki is a genuine third outcome for a local fight, distinct from either group living outright or dying.
seki.elaboration: Seki matters for scoring because it is handled differently, in detail, by different rulesets, which is exactly the kind of parameter the rulesets comparison exists to pin down. Under territory scoring, the shared liberties inside a seki count as points for neither player and stones in seki earn no prisoner value, since nothing was captured. Under area scoring, each side's own stones in the seki count as that side's area as normal, while the shared liberties still count for neither side, since they are not enclosed exclusively by one color.

related.title: life-and-death
related.note: Seki is the standoff outcome that arises specifically when neither side's life-and-death reading resolves in its favor.

related.title: eye
related.note: Groups in seki characteristically lack the two eyes that would make them unconditionally alive.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Seki is defined by a shared, unfillable pool of liberties between opposing groups.

related.title: area-scoring
related.note: Area scoring counts each seki group's own stones but not the shared liberties between them.

related.title: territory-scoring
related.note: Territory scoring credits neither side with the shared liberties inside a seki.

semeai.title: semeai
semeai.definition: Semeai ("capturing race") in weiqi is a contest between two adjacent groups, neither of which has secured two eyes, where each side fills the other's liberties as fast as possible and the group that runs out first is captured. It differs from an ordinary atari chase because both groups are mutually vulnerable at once — the racing side must count whether it can fill the opponent's last liberty before its own runs out, not merely whether it can force the opponent into atari.
semeai.elaboration: Counting a semeai correctly is exact, countable work: shared liberties, approach moves, and whether either group has an eye that must be filled last all change the count in specific, computable ways rather than by rough estimation. A semeai miscounted by even one liberty reverses which side survives.

related.title: liberty
related.note: A semeai is decided entirely by counting liberties on both sides of the race.

related.title: atari
related.note: A semeai is the mutual, two-sided generalization of the one-sided pressure atari names.

related.title: life-and-death
related.note: A semeai is a life-and-death question between two groups at once, rather than one group reading against an empty board.

sente.title: sente
sente.definition: Sente in weiqi is the initiative: a move the opponent must answer, so that the player who made it may play again elsewhere. Gote is its complement, a move that ends the mover's turn because the opponent need not answer. A sequence is sente for a player if that player retains the initiative through it.
sente.elaboration: Sente is already mathematized, and well. Berlekamp and Wolfe's combinatorial-game-theory treatment of the Go endgame decomposes a position into a disjunctive sum of independent local games; each has a *temperature*, roughly the value of moving there first; optimal play takes the hottest available game; and the sente/gote distinction falls out of that temperature structure rather than needing a separate definition. This is exact for the class of endgame positions the book treats, and the section's own research does not attempt to re-derive it: CGT owns this ground.

related.title: gote
related.note: Gote is the complementary state: a move the opponent need not answer.

related.title: miai
related.note: Miai points are settled precisely because neither side needs sente to secure one of them.

related.title: honte
related.note: Honte is the solid move played at the cost of the tempo sente would have kept.

related.title: aji
related.note: Unlike aji, sente's value is spent the moment the opponent answers, not held open.

suicide.title: suicide
suicide.definition: Suicide in weiqi is a move that would leave the moving player's own stone or group with zero liberties after any opposing stones it removes are taken off the board. Under most rulesets suicide is simply illegal: a player may not place a stone that reduces their own group to no liberties unless that same move first captures an opposing group and thereby restores at least one liberty. New Zealand rules are the well-known exception, permitting suicide of any size — a player may play a stone, or fill their own group's last liberties entirely, and the played stones are then immediately removed as self-captured.
suicide.elaboration: Suicide is worth distinguishing carefully from an ordinary capture that happens to leave the capturing stone momentarily surrounded: legality is checked by removing captured opponent stones first, then checking the mover's own liberties, so a move that captures is never suicide even if, before the capture is applied, it looked like it had none. Suicide also differs from ko: a ko recapture always removes exactly one opposing stone and is judged by the repetition rule, while suicide by definition captures nothing at all.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Suicide is defined directly in terms of a move reducing the mover's own liberties to zero.

related.title: capture
related.note: A move is never suicide if it captures an opposing group first, since capture is checked before self-liberties.

related.title: eye
related.note: Rulesets that forbid suicide are the reason a genuine single-point eye cannot legally be filled by the opponent without first capturing around it.

related.title: ko
related.note: Ko recaptures and suicide are easy to confuse; ko always captures one stone, suicide by definition captures none.

superko.title: superko
superko.definition: Superko in weiqi is a repetition rule that extends ko beyond the single immediately-preceding position: it forbids recreating *any* whole-board position that has already occurred in the game, not only the one position just before the opponent's last move. Two variants are in common use. Positional superko (PSK) forbids any recurrence of an identical arrangement of stones, regardless of whose turn it is. Situational superko (SSK) forbids a recurrence only when it is also the same player's turn to move as it was the earlier time that arrangement occurred — so the same stone arrangement may legally recur once with the other player to move, but not a second time with the original player to move.
superko.elaboration: Superko matters because the simple ko rule alone only blocks immediate two-move recaptures; it does nothing to stop longer cycles, such as triple ko or other multi-ko patterns, from repeating a board position indefinitely and preventing the game from ever concluding. Superko rules close that gap by treating repetition of the whole board, not just of one local point, as the thing to forbid. Which variant a ruleset adopts is one of the parameters recorded in the rulesets comparison, since Chinese-tradition and New Zealand rules typically use positional superko while AGA rules specify situational superko, and Japanese rules historically rely on simple ko alone plus an ad hoc "no result" convention for unresolved long cycles.

related.title: ko
related.note: Superko generalizes the simple ko rule from one forbidden position to all previously occurring positions.

related.title: capture
related.note: Superko violations can only arise from sequences of captures and recaptures, since placement alone never restores an earlier board.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Long ko cycles that superko must adjudicate arise from groups repeatedly reduced to and restored from a shared last liberty.

related.title: seki
related.note: Some multi-ko fights that superko must resolve are closely related to seki: neither side can safely play the deciding capture.

sute-ishi.title: sute-ishi
sute-ishi.definition: Sute-ishi ("throw-away stones") in weiqi are one or more stones deliberately played to be captured, because the exchange the capture forces is worth more than the stones would have been worth kept alive. The player plans the loss before the opponent takes it; the stones are bait, not a mistake later rationalized as sacrifice.
sute-ishi.elaboration: A sacrifice earns its keep in one of a few standard ways: it draws the opponent into spending moves capturing low-value stones while the sacrificing player builds thickness or territory elsewhere, it keeps sente by forcing a specific, predictable response, or it removes a cutting point the opponent would otherwise have exploited. Sute-ishi is a plan for the whole exchange, not a description of any single stone; the same stone that looks sacrificed in isolation may in fact need to survive if the surrounding reading changes.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Sabaki treats a group's own stones as expendable in the same way sute-ishi treats bait stones as expendable, applied to settling a whole group rather than one exchange.

related.title: aji
related.note: A sacrificed stone frequently leaves aji behind even after capture, rather than disappearing from the position's latent options entirely.

related.title: sente
related.note: A well-timed sacrifice is a common way to keep sente: the opponent must answer by capturing rather than tenuki.

territory-scoring.title: territory-scoring
territory-scoring.definition: Territory scoring in weiqi computes each player's final score as the vacant points that count as that player's territory plus the prisoners that player captured from the opponent during the game; a live stone remaining on the board at the end contributes no direct point value of its own. Japanese and Korean rules use territory scoring. Because stones themselves are not counted, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs a full point under territory scoring: it removes one territory point and, since nothing was captured, adds nothing back.
territory-scoring.elaboration: That cost is the main practical difference from area-scoring, and it is one reason experienced players under territory scoring stop playing inside their own territory as soon as a group is settled, while players under area scoring can fill such points for free. The exact standard komi and other parameters for each ruleset are recorded in the rulesets comparison.

related.title: territory
related.note: Territory scoring's core term is the vacant points a player's stones enclose.

related.title: area-scoring
related.note: Territory scoring and area scoring are the two families of final-count rule a ruleset must choose between.

related.title: komi
related.note: Standard komi values differ between territory-scoring and area-scoring rulesets partly to offset how each counts stones.

related.title: dead-stones
related.note: Territory-scoring rulesets typically resolve dead stones by mutual agreement after passing.

related.title: capture
related.note: Captures matter directly under territory scoring, since prisoners are added to the final count.

territory.title: territory
territory.definition: Territory in weiqi is the set of vacant points effectively enclosed by one player's stones and unavailable to the opponent except at unacceptable cost.
territory.elaboration: Territory is the strategic heart of the game because it turns placement into scoring. A move may increase territory directly by closing space, or indirectly by making an invasion weak. This is why players often choose moves that neither attack nor defend a single group immediately but instead reshape the balance of large empty regions.

related.title: liberty
related.note: Territory remains meaningful only if the surrounding stones retain enough liberties to hold it.

related.title: capture
related.note: Captures can secure or destroy territory by changing which stones remain on the board.

related.title: komi
related.note: Komi adjusts final scores after territory has been counted.

related.title: ko
related.note: Ko fights can determine whether a key territorial area remains secure.

thickness.title: thickness
thickness.definition: Thickness (*atsumi*) in weiqi is a strong, settled, outward-facing formation with no weakness the opponent can exploit locally. Three classical maxims describe what thickness is not: do not use it to enclose territory, since walling off space wastes the wall's real value; do not play close to thickness, yours or the opponent's, since stones near a thick wall are cheap for its owner to attack; and thickness is a property of the position, not of the stones, so the same wall is strong against an empty board and worthless once the opponent has a living group settled behind it.
thickness.elaboration: That third maxim is the one with formal content: a wall's thickness can be destroyed without the wall itself being touched. If the opponent settles a group nearby, the stones of the wall are unchanged and its thickness is gone. A **wall** is the shape; thickness is the shape's value in context.

related.title: influence
related.note: Thickness is influence concentrated into one strong, settled wall.

related.title: honte
related.note: Building thickness and playing honte are both trades of tempo for a position with no local weakness.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Sabaki is the light, expendable-stone strategy for operating near an opponent's thickness rather than confronting it directly.

related.title: territory
related.note: Enclosing territory with a thick wall is the classical waste of thickness's real value.

tobi.title: tobi
tobi.definition: Tobi ("jump") in weiqi is playing a stone one empty point away from an existing stone along a line, leaving the intersection between them unoccupied. A two-space jump extends the same idea one point further; both are not physically connected the way an adjacent stone is, but are functionally connected in most fighting situations because the opponent cutting at the gap usually costs more than it gains.
tobi.elaboration: Tobi is a light shape: it covers more of the board per stone than a solid connection does, at the cost of leaving a cutting point the opponent can sometimes exploit. Whether a given jump's gap is a real weakness or only a theoretical one is a local reading question, not something the shape settles by itself.

related.title: keima
related.note: Keima is the other standard light-extension shape, covering a different offset than tobi at a similar cost in connection strength.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Jumps are the characteristic move of sabaki play, trading a firm connection for speed and flexibility.

related.title: dango
related.note: Tobi is the light alternative to the heavy, over-connected shape dango names.

zenkyoku.title: zenkyoku
zenkyoku.definition: Zenkyoku ("whole board") in weiqi is evaluating a move by its effect on the balance of the entire board rather than judging the local exchange in isolation. A move read as locally correct can still be the wrong move once its effect on a distant, seemingly unrelated group is counted; zenkyoku is the discipline of checking that effect before playing.
zenkyoku.elaboration: As a proposal of this section's own Whole-Board Reading as a Gluing Problem, and Lineages as Signatures (§1, §4), zenkyoku names exactly the reading a purely regional strategy lacks: the article reads a regional strategy's failure to account for a distant effect as a cover-nerve coordination obstruction, and reads whole-board play as a distribution over the readout space that couples regions a local reading would treat as independent. Status: proposal.

related.title: aji
related.note: Zenkyoku frequently means holding a local option open specifically because of the effect it has elsewhere on the board.

related.title: miai
related.note: Recognizing miai points requires the same whole-board comparison zenkyoku names, applied to two equivalent points rather than one distant effect.

related.title: sabaki
related.note: Light, quickly-settled shape is what lets a player disengage from one region and act on a whole-board reading elsewhere.
